transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you here today?

Well, I suppose... I just don’t have the push I used to have. Like for choir, or my quilting, or visiting folks. I used to make these big star pattern quilts. My grandmother taught me how when I was just a little girl, using old flour sacks, if you can believe it. You can't even get cotton like that anymore, everything at the store now is so thin and it frays before you even get a needle through it. 

But... what was I saying? Oh, right. I just don't have the energy for it anymore. Most days I just sit at home in my chair. I leave the TV on real low... usually on that channel that plays the old game shows. Bob Barker, you know, he was such a handsome man back in the day, always had that nice tan. But I just sit there with the volume down, even though I know people are expecting me at the church or at the quilting circle. I just can't seem to get myself out the door.
How long have you been feeling this way, without much energy or interest in doing things?

Well, I suppose it's been building up for a while now. Ever since I retired from the school office, which was... oh, a little over two years ago, I think. I used to answer the phones there and help the little ones when they felt sick. The children were always losing their lunchboxes or forgetting their winter coats. You wouldn't believe the things they'd leave behind. 

One time, a little boy left a glass jar with a real live frog in it right on my front desk. Just sitting there looking at me! My brother Tommy caught a frog like that once when we were little, and he put it right in my mother's flour bin. Oh, she was so mad... she chased him clear across the yard with her heavy wooden mixing spoon. She had this big oak spoon she used for making bread, and she wouldn't let anyone else wash it because she said soap would ruin the wood... 

I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, about the energy. Yes, it's just been getting worse since I left the school, about two years ago.
Do you feel down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

Depressed? Well, no, I wouldn't say sad. I don't sit around crying or feeling blue or anything like that. Now, my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she was depressed. She cried every single day when her little dog passed away. It was a Pomeranian, I think. Nasty little thing, really, always nipping at my ankles when I'd walk out to the box to get the mail. The mail carrier we had back then, his name was Ricky, and he was just terrified of that dog. Ricky always wore those blue uniform shorts, even in the dead of winter when there was thick frost on the ground. I used to ask him if his knees were freezing off, and he would just laugh. He had such a loud laugh, you could hear it three houses down... 

But no, I don't feel down like that. Just... like I said, I just don't have the push to do much.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to think clearly or concentrate on tasks lately?

Think clearly? Well, I suppose my mind is still working just fine. I haven't noticed any trouble with that. I can still do the word search in the Sunday paper without much fuss. Though I swear, that paper boy throws it right into the rose bushes half the time. I have to go out there in my slippers and fish it out of the thorns. Those bushes have been there since my husband planted them... oh, it must have been 1982. He bought them at the old hardware store downtown, the one with the green awning. It burned down a few years back, which was such a shame. They used to sell nails loose out of a big wooden barrel, and they smelled like... well, like old iron and machine oil. You just scooped out what you needed and weighed them on this big brass scale. The man who worked there, Mr. Henderson, he always had an unlit cigar tucked right behind his ear. I never once saw him smoke it, just kept it sitting right there behind his glasses... 

But, oh, what were we talking about? My thinking? Yes, no, my thinking is fine. Just the push to do things is gone, like I said.
Do you feel that you have less energy or motivation to do things compared to how you used to be?

Yes, that's exactly it. That's really what brings me in, to be honest. I just don't have the push I used to have for things like choir, or my quilting group, or visiting folks. I used to love quilting. I made a beautiful double-wedding-ring pattern for my sister's girl when she got married. The wedding was out in a barn, if you can believe it. People pay good money to get married in a drafty old barn these days! They had these little glass mason jars with candles in them hanging from the wooden rafters. Well, one of the ropes snapped and a jar fell and nearly caught a bale of hay on fire. The groom's uncle had to stomp it out with his dress shoes. He ruined a perfectly good pair of patent leather loafers. I always told my husband you should never wear nice shoes to a farm. My father used to keep his old green rubber boots by the back door, always covered in muck, and my mother would holler if he even stepped one foot onto her clean kitchen linoleum... 

Oh, my mind is wandering again, isn't it? I'm sorry. But yes, about the energy. I just don't have it. Instead of going out to quilt or sing, most days I just sit at home with the TV on low. I don't even really watch it, it's just flickering there. I know people are expecting me at the church and wondering where I am, but I just can't seem to find the push to get out the door anymore.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, like choir, quilting, or visiting people?

Well, yes, like I was just saying a minute ago, that's really what brings me in. It's not even about whether I enjoy them or not, I just... I just don't have the push I used to have for the choir, or the quilting, or visiting folks. Instead of going, most days I just sit at home with the TV on low. I know people are expecting me, especially at church. Pastor Miller is probably looking out at the pews wondering where I am. 

He always wears these terrible plaid ties, you know. I don't know who buys his ties for him, probably his wife, Susan. Now, Susan makes a wonderful potato salad. She puts a little bit of yellow mustard and celery seed in hers, which gives it a nice tang. I tried to make it just like hers once for a church picnic back in... oh, it must have been the summer of '98. We had the picnic down by the lake, and the ducks kept coming right up to our blanket, bold as brass. One of those ducks actually snatched a whole hotdog bun right out of my cousin Arthur's hand! Arthur was so mad, he chased that duck all the way down to the muddy bank, waving his paper plate around. He slipped and got mud all over his good trousers. His wife was just furious with him, making him ride all the way home sitting on a plastic garbage bag so he wouldn't ruin the car seats... 

But anyway, what was the question? Enjoyment? Yes, I just don't have the push for any of it anymore. Just the TV on low.
Do you still get pleasure out of things like watching TV, even if you don’t feel like doing much else?

Pleasure? No, I wouldn't say that. Like I said, it's just on. I don't really pay it any mind, it just sits there flickering. I think it's usually just stuck on that channel that plays the old game shows in the afternoon. 

My sister actually won a prize on a radio contest once, back in... oh, it must have been the seventies. She won a beautiful chrome toaster. Four slots! We thought we were high society with a four-slot toaster. We'd go down to the corner market and buy that thick sliced bread just to use it. The man who ran the market, Mr. Gable, he had this big old basset hound that just slept right in the middle of the aisle. You had to step right over him to get to the canned peaches. That dog must have weighed eighty pounds, just a big lump of wrinkles and floppy ears. He smelled awful, too, like wet old rugs, but Mr. Gable loved him like a son. He used to feed him pieces of bologna right out of the deli case. I always thought that was a health code violation, but nobody ever reported him. 

I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, the TV. No, it doesn't really give me any joy. It's just noise in the room.
Have you found yourself feeling like you're not worth much or that you're letting people down lately?

Well... no, I wouldn't say I feel like I'm not worth much. I don't really have those kinds of thoughts. I mean, I know I'm letting the folks at church down by not showing up, but it's not like I sit here beating myself up about it. 

My mother, though, she used to be terribly hard on herself. If she burned the Sunday roast, she wouldn't speak for the rest of the afternoon. We had this old gas stove, a real beast of a thing. It had these heavy iron grates on top that took two hands to lift when you had to scrub underneath them. My brother Thomas once dropped one of those grates right on his big toe. Oh, he howled! He was wearing just his socks, those thick wool ones with the red stripe at the top. He had to wear an open-toed sandal to school for two weeks in November. The teacher, Miss Higgins, she made him sit right by the radiator so his foot wouldn't freeze. She was a strict woman, Miss Higgins. Always wore her hair in a tight bun that looked like it gave her a headache. She used to rap her ruler on the chalkboard if anyone so much as whispered...

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, about letting people down. No, I don't really feel worthless or anything like that. Just... tired.
Have there been times when you felt down or really didn’t care about things as much as you used to, even things you used to enjoy?

Well, I suppose I have been feeling down, yes. I just don't have the energy to care about much of anything anymore. I used to care about keeping the house tidy, but now the dust just gathers. 

Dust is a funny thing, isn't it? It just appears out of nowhere. My grandmother used to say dust was just dead skin, which is a horrible thought. She was full of horrible thoughts like that. She grew up on a farm in the Dakotas, you see. The winters there were brutal. She used to tell us stories about having to tie a rope from the back door to the barn so they wouldn't get lost in the snowdrifts when they went to milk the cows. One year, the snow was so high it buried the whole first floor of the house. They had to climb out a second-story window just to see the sky! Can you imagine? Climbing out a window into a mountain of snow. Her brother, my great-uncle Henry, he tried to dig a tunnel through it, but it collapsed on him. He was fine, just got a terrible cold that settled in his chest. He always had a wheeze after that. Sounded like an old accordion when he laughed...

I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, feeling down. Yes, I suppose I do feel down. I just don't care about things the way I used to.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

Well... I don't know if it's most of the day, every day. It's hard to keep track of time lately. The days just sort of blend together, you know? Like soup. 

My aunt Martha used to make the most wonderful split pea soup. She'd simmer it on the stove all day with a big ham bone. The whole house would smell like it. She had this enormous cast-iron pot, must have weighed twenty pounds empty. She bought it at a rummage sale at the Methodist church back in... oh, 1982, I think. That church had the best rummage sales. People would line up down the block before the doors even opened. One time, my cousin Betty found a genuine mink stole for three dollars! Three dollars! It had a little tear in the lining, but nobody could see that. She wore it to Sunday service every week until she spilled communion wine on it. Red wine on white mink, it was a tragedy. She tried to wash it in the sink with dish soap, but it just got stiff and matted. Looked like a drowned rat after that... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, feeling depressed every day. I don't really know. I just feel tired and flat, I suppose. I haven't really been paying attention to how many hours a day it is.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

Well, I think I just said... I don't really know if it's every single day. The days are just so long now. They stretch out like... like taffy. 

Did you ever go to the boardwalk and watch them pull taffy? They have those big metal machines with the arms that just stretch it and fold it, stretch it and fold it. We used to go to the shore every summer when I was a girl. My father would rent this little cottage that always smelled a bit like mildew and old sunscreen. But we didn't care. We'd spend all day on the beach building sandcastles. My sister, she was always trying to build these elaborate moats, but the tide would always come in and wash them away. She'd get so mad, she'd stomp her little feet and her pigtails would bounce. She had the most beautiful blonde hair, just like spun gold. My mother used to brush it for a hundred strokes every night before bed. She read somewhere in a magazine that it made the hair shine. Women's Day, I think it was. Or maybe Good Housekeeping. They always had those little tips for housewives in the back pages, right next to the recipes for casseroles made with cream of mushroom soup...

What was I... oh, right. The days. I don't know about most of the day. I just feel flat. I really haven't been keeping track.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

I feel like you're asking me the exact same thing again. Like I said, I don't know if it's every single day or most of the day. I just feel flat. It's like my head is just... empty. 

Empty heads... that makes me think of those scarecrows we used to make in the fall. We'd stuff old clothes with straw and leaves. We had this one pair of overalls, they belonged to my grandfather before he passed, and we'd use them every year. They had a big patch on the left knee where he tore them on a barbed wire fence. He was trying to chase a stray calf that got out of the pasture. That calf was a menace, always finding the weak spot in the fence. He named it Houdini. Anyway, the scarecrows never really scared the crows. The crows were too smart. They'd just sit right on the scarecrow's hat and caw at us. They're very intelligent birds, crows. I read once they can remember human faces. Imagine that, a bird remembering you. I wonder what they think of us. Probably that we're very silly creatures, always rushing around, stuffing straw into old clothes...

I'm sorry, I don't know what else to tell you about the days. I just haven't been keeping track of the hours.
Have you found that you’ve lost interest or pleasure in almost everything, even things you used to really enjoy?

Well, I suppose so. That's actually what brings me in... I just don't have the push I used to have for things. Like my choir, or my quilting group. I used to love quilting. We'd sit around for hours, piecing together the squares. 

My grandmother taught me how to quilt when I was just a little thing. She had this old treadle sewing machine. You had to pump the pedal with your feet to make the needle go. It made this rhythmic clicking sound, click-clack, click-clack. She made a beautiful double wedding ring quilt for my parents when they got married. The fabrics were all scraps from old dresses and shirts, so every piece had a story. There was a little square of blue gingham from a dress she wore to a barn dance in 1941. That was the year the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor, you know. Everyone was so scared. My uncle Henry enlisted the very next day. He was stationed in the Pacific, on a destroyer. He sent back these letters written on thin, crinkly paper that folded up into their own envelopes. V-mail, they called it. He brought back a real silk kimono for my aunt when the war was over. It was red, with golden dragons embroidered all over it...

Anyway, I don't go to quilting anymore, or visiting folks. Most days I just sit at home with the TV on low. I know people are expecting me, but I just don't have the energy to get up and go.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

Doctor, are you feeling alright? You just asked me that exact same thing again. Like a broken record. I really don't know how else to explain it to you... I don't feel sad or down all day. I just feel flat. 

Speaking of broken records, my brother Tommy used to have this little portable record player in his bedroom. He bought a 45 of Johnny Cash, and he played it so many times it got a deep scratch right in the vinyl. It would just skip and play the exact same guitar twang over and over and over. Drove my father absolutely up the wall. He threatened to throw the whole machine out the kitchen window, right into the tomato garden. 

Daddy grew the biggest beefsteak tomatoes you ever saw. He'd tie the vines up to these tall wooden stakes with strips of my mother's old pantyhose. He read somewhere that the nylon was gentler on the stems than regular twine, so it wouldn't cut into the plant when the tomatoes got heavy. We'd slice them thick in August, put a little salt and mayonnaise on white bread... best sandwich in the world. We'd eat them out on the porch swing because the house was always too hot with the oven off. You had to lean forward so the tomato juice didn't drip down your chin onto your good shirt...

But no, to answer your question, I'm not crying or depressed every day. It's just that empty feeling I told you about.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

Are you... are you sure you're okay, doctor? You're asking me the same question for the third time now. I really don't know what else to say. I'm not sad. I'm just empty. 

Empty like... well, like the old water tower out past the county line. They drained it years ago when they put in the new reservoir. It's just sitting out there, rusting away. My cousins and I used to dare each other to climb the ladder on the side. It was so high up, you could see all the way to the interstate. One time, my cousin Bobby climbed all the way to the top and carved his initials into the metal. B.J.W. Bobby James Wilcox. He was always getting into trouble. He joined the Navy right out of high school, just to get away from his dad. His dad was a harsh man, worked at the lumber mill down by the river. The mill shut down in the eighties, though. Everyone lost their jobs. It was a real hard time for the town. People were packing up and leaving left and right. Just empty houses everywhere...

But like I said, I'm not depressed or crying all the time. I just don't have anything in me right now.

He was wearing just his socks, those thick wool ones with the red stripe at the top. He had to wear an open-toed sandal to school for two weeks in November. The teacher, Miss Higgins, she made him sit right by the radiator so his foot wouldn't freeze. She was a strict woman, Miss Higgins. She had this enormous cast-iron pot, must have weighed twenty pounds empty. She bought it at a rummage sale at the Methodist church back in... oh, 1982, I think. That church had the best rummage sales. People would line up down the block before the doors even opened. One time, my cousin Betty found a genuine mink stole for three dollars! Three dollars! It had a little tear in the lining, but nobody could see that. She wore it to Sunday service every week until she spilled communion wine on it. Red wine on white mink, it was a tragedy. She tried to wash it in the sink with dish soap, but it just got stiff and matted. Looked like a drowned rat after that...

My mother used to brush it for a hundred strokes every night before bed. She read somewhere in a magazine that it made the hair shine. Women's Day, I think it was. Or maybe Good Housekeeping. They always had those little tips for housewives in the back pages, right next to the recipes for casseroles made with cream of mushroom soup...

What was I... oh, right. The days. I don't know about most of the day. I just feel flat. I really haven't been keeping track.

Anyway, the scarecrows never really scared the crows. The crows were too smart. They'd just sit right on the scarecrow's hat and caw at us. They're very intelligent birds, crows. Well, I suppose so. That's actually what brings me in... I just don't have the push I used to have for things. Like my choir, or my quilting group. I used to love quilting. We'd sit around for hours, piecing together the squares. 

My grandmother taught me how to quilt when I was just a little thing. She had this old treadle sewing machine. You had to pump the pedal with your feet to make the needle go. It made this rhythmic clicking sound, click-clack, click-clack. She made a beautiful double wedding ring quilt for my parents when they got married. The fabrics were all scraps from old dresses and shirts, so every piece had a story. There was a little square of blue gingham from a dress she wore to a barn dance in 1941. That was the year the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor, you know. Everyone was so scared. My uncle Henry enlisted the very next day. He was stationed in the Pacific, on a destroyer. He sent back these letters written on thin, crinkly paper that folded up into their own envelopes. V-mail, they called it. He brought back a real silk kimono for my aunt when the war was over. It was red, with golden dragons embroidered all over it...
